profile.name: Tripuri dance
profile.tagline: Agricultural, ritual, and hunting dances of the indigenous hill communities of Tripura.
profile.insight: During the April sowing season, Tripuri dancers move from village to village to drums and flutes, accelerating their tempo to mimic the natural world.
profile.profile: Tripuri dance encompasses a broad family of traditional folk, sacred, and occupational dances performed by the Tripuri people and related communities such as the Reangs, Marmas, and Halams in northeastern India. Deeply rooted in jhum (shifting) cultivation, these dances mark key agricultural milestones from sowing during Garia Puja to post-harvest celebrations like Mamita and Hai-hak. They also include specialized ritual and occupational forms, such as the Reang clan's Hojagiri balancing dance and the insect-attracting Lebang Boomani. Music relies on traditional instruments like the khamb drum, pung percussion, bamboo clappers, flutes, and the stringed sarinda.
profile.profile_long:
Tripuri dance represents the collective performance traditions of the indigenous tribal communities residing in the hill regions of Tripura in northeastern India. Dominated by the Tripuri ethnic group—who make up over half of the state's tribal population—alongside the Reang, Marma (Mog), and Halam communities, these dances reflect an intimate bond with the landscape, agricultural cycles, and traditional spiritual life. Central to their social organization is jhum, or shifting hill cultivation, around which the seasonal calendar of festivals and community performances revolves.

The dance traditions span a variety of distinct forms tied to specific seasons, rituals, and communities. The Goria (or Garia) dance takes place during the Garia Puja in April to mark the commencement of the crop sowing season. Accompanied by drums and flutes, mixed-gender groups move from village to village in a performance that gradually increases in tempo, using hand mudras to mimic nature and petition the deities for a bountiful harvest. Following the sowing, during the lull before the monsoon, the Lebang Boomani dance is performed to manage the influx of lebangs—colorful insects that descend upon the slopes to feed on sown seeds. In this dance, men strike bamboo clappers called tokkas to create a rhythmic sound believed to draw the insects out, while women wave bright scarves to catch them, using the count of caught insects to predict harvest abundance.

Harvest times bring additional celebratory and sacred dances. The Mamita dance is executed during the Mamita harvest festival, while the Hai-hak dance is performed specifically by the Halam community to honor the goddess Lakshmi at her place of worship after the annual harvest. Distinct clan-based traditions also flourish: the Hojagiri dance of the Reang clan features young women balancing props such as earthen pitchers or bottles on their heads and lamps on their hands while strictly restricting movement to the lower half of the body. Occupational and seasonal rituals are further represented by Mosak sulmani, an ancient hunting dance that mimics the tracking and capturing of game through stylized gestures, as well as the Buddhist traditions of the Marma (Mog) community, including the Sangrai dance performed during Chaitra (April) and the Owa dance celebrated during the full moon of Ashwin.

Across these varied forms, traditional attire and instrumentation maintain cultural cohesion. Female dancers often adorn themselves with silver chains, rings, bangles, and bronze ear and nose rings. The music relies on indigenous regional instruments, including the khamb drum, pung percussion, bamboo tokkas, bamboo flutes, and the stringed sarinda. Through public national showcases—such as the Marma community's Sangrai dance featured during India's Republic Day parade on Rajpath on January 26, 2018—these hill traditions continue to maintain active visibility while anchoring local community life.

sections.origins_and_history: Tripuri dance originated among the indigenous tribal communities living in the hills of Tripura in northeastern India, predominantly the Tripuri people who constitute over half of the tribal population, alongside the Reangs, Marmas (Mogs), and Halams. The dances historically evolved around jhum (shifting cultivation) and seasonal agrarian rituals. Over time, specific clan traditions developed, such as the Reang clan's Hojagiri dance and the Marma community's Sangrai and Owa dances. On 26 January 2018, the Sangrai dance of the Mog tribe was showcased for the first time on Rajpath during India's Republic Day parade.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance structure varies by specific tradition. The Goria dance is performed by both men and women moving village to village in a gradually increasing tempo using mudras that mimic natural movements. In the Reang clan's Hojagiri dance, teams of four to six young women balance props like bottles or earthen pitchers on their heads and lamps on their hands while moving only the lower half of the body. In the Lebang Boomani dance, men operate bamboo tokka clappers to create rhythmic beats while women wave colorful scarves to enact catching insects. Mosak sulmani uses elaborate physical gestures to mimic hunting acts.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tripuri dances are accompanied by regional indigenous musical instruments. Sowing and general folk dances like Goria use drums and flutes. Lebang Boomani incorporates bamboo clappers called tokkas alongside the flute, the khamb drum, the pung percussion instrument, and the sarinda string instrument. Songs accompany balancing forms like Hojagiri, where teams of four to six members sing while performing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers perform in outdoor village spaces, hill slopes, places of worship, and temples. For dances like Lebang Boomani, women adorn themselves with silver chains, rings, and bangles, along with bronze ear and nose rings, while carrying colorful scarves. In Hojagiri, dancers balance props such as earthen pitchers, bottles, and lit or unlit lamps. Marma Buddhist dances such as Owa are performed in connection with visits to Buddhist temples and river sites where paper or toy boats are launched.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are tied to the agricultural calendar, seasonal shifts, and religious observances. Goria dance accompanies prayers during April's Garia Puja for a bountiful crop. Lebang Boomani is performed during the pre-monsoon lull; the number of lebang insects caught is believed to indicate harvest prosperity. Post-harvest dances include Mamita and the Halam community's Hai-hak dance, performed to honor the goddess Lakshmi. The Marma community's Owa dance takes place on the full moon day of Ashwin in the Bengali calendar, and Sangrai occurs during the month of April (Chaitra). Mosak sulmani serves as a hunting ritual dance.
sections.regional_variants: Variants correspond to ethnic communities within Tripura. The Tripuri group practices Goria, Lebang Boomani, Mamita, and Jhum dance. The Reang clan performs the Hojagiri balancing dance. The Halam community performs the Hai-hak dance for Lakshmi. The Marma (Mog) community practices the Sangrai dance and the Buddhist Owa dance.
sections.lineage: Tripuri dance belongs to the traditional folk and ritual dance lineages of northeastern India, originating from the jhum-cultivating tribal groups of Tripura including the Tripuri, Reang, Halam, and Marma communities.

profile.sacred_note: Several Tripuri dances are sacred rituals performed during religious festivals and at places of worship, such as the Goria dance during Garia Puja, the Hai-hak dance at goddess Lakshmi's place of worship, and the Marma community's Buddhist Owa dance.

basic_steps: Gradual tempo shift from slow step-touch to rapid rhythmic footwork (Goria)
Tokka bamboo clapper striking pattern by male dancers (Lebang Boomani)
Scarf waving in rhythmic sweeping paths to capture imaginary insects (Lebang Boomani)
Lower-body isolated hip and sway movements while keeping the upper torso rigid and balancing head props (Hojagiri)
teaching.rhythm: Varies by form; driven by khamb drums, pung percussion, bamboo clappers, and flutes with gradually increasing tempo.
teaching.formation: Mixed-gender lines or processional groups moving village to village (Goria); teams of 4 to 6 women (Hojagiri); paired gender groups (Lebang Boomani).
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic step patterns and clapper rhythms of Lebang Boomani or Goria before attempting lower-body isolation and object balancing in Hojagiri.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Rhythmic bamboo clapper striking (tokka) coupled with steady khamb and pung percussion beats that accelerate progressively.
music_profile.vocal_style: Group unison singing by team members accompanying performance.
music_profile.musical_form: Strophic rhythmic framework that gradually accelerates in tempo.
music_profile.sound_description: A vibrant acoustic blend dominated by the sharp, repetitive crack of bamboo tokka clappers, deep resonant thuds of khamb and pung percussion, melismatically floating bamboo flute melodies, and high-pitched sarinda strings.

movement_profile.posture: Varies from erect torso holding balance with lower-body isolation (Hojagiri) to fluid, bending stances mimicking agricultural acts and nature (Lebang Boomani, Mosak sulmani).
movement_profile.footwork: Progressive village-to-village walking steps that build in tempo; localized lower-body swaying and stepping.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Hand mudras mimicking natural elements; waving colorful scarves; balancing lamps on hands; striking bamboo clappers.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Isolated lower-body motion in Hojagiri while torso remains stationary to support head props; fluid natural torso sways in Lebang Boomani.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Processions moving across village terrain; small group floor patterns of 4 to 6 members.
movement_profile.partnering: Complementary gender roles where men manage rhythm instruments/clappers and women perform prop/scarf movement.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Accelerating from a steady initial tempo to a fast peak.

signature_moves.name: Tokka Clapping
signature_moves.description: Men striking bamboo clappers rhythmically to attract insects.

signature_moves.name: Lebang Scarf Catch
signature_moves.description: Women waving bright scarves through the air to catch flying insects.

signature_moves.name: Prop Balancing Lower Isolation
signature_moves.description: Reang women swaying hips and moving lower body while balancing bottles, pitchers, or lamps.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Primarily grounded stepping and swaying; minimal high jumping.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid sudden head movements during balancing routines; do not disassociate upper and lower body isolations during prop balancing.

learning_units.description: Tokka clapper beat coordination with step movement.

episode_brief.title_hook: Rhythms of the Jhum Hills: The Dances of Tripura
episode_brief.logline: Explore how the indigenous hill communities of Tripura transform agricultural life and sacred rituals into vibrant music and movement.
beats: Opening on the hill slopes of Tripura during April's Garia Puja sowing festival.
Demonstration of the bamboo tokka clappers creating rhythmic beats to lure lebang insects.
The scarf-waving Lebang Boomani dance depicting the seasonal insect harvest.
Focus on the Reang clan's Hojagiri performance featuring extreme balance and lower-body movement.
Concluding with the Marma community's riverfront Owa festival boat launching.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the tokka bamboo clapper rhythm and basic step-touch movement.
drills: Step-touch walking with gradual tempo increase

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute the Lebang Boomani scarf-waving pattern in harmony with clappers.
drills: Synchronized partner stepping and scarf sweeping

lesson_ladder.goal: Practice lower-body isolation while maintaining head stability.
drills: Lower-body hip swaying while isolating upper torso

episode_brief.instructor_persona: An engaging documentary presenter visiting village elders and community practitioners in the Tripura hills.
episode_brief.music_cue: Ensemble of khamb drum, bamboo flute, and tokka clappers building from a soft slow rhythm to an energetic crescendo.
